properties.name: Montauk Club
properties.description: A Venetian Gothic social club designed by Francis H. Kimball and completed in 1891, ornamented in terra cotta with scenes of the Montauk people. A New York City landmark at 25 Eighth Avenue and Lincoln Place.
properties.photoAlt: The Montauk Club photographed from Eighth Avenue around 1910
properties.photoCredit: Eugene L. Armbruster, c. 1910 · Center for Brooklyn History (public domain)

properties.name: Obama's Brownstone
properties.description: 640 2nd Street, a 1901 brownstone on a Prospect Park block. In late 1984, fresh out of Columbia, Barack Obama shared the top-floor apartment here with his girlfriend Genevieve Cook before moving to Manhattan the following spring.
properties.photoAlt: The full brownstone facade of 640 Second Street in Park Slope, where Obama lived
properties.photoCredit: Real-estate listing photo of 640 Second Street

properties.name: 1960 Plane Crash Site
properties.description: On December 16, 1960, a United Air Lines DC-8 collided in midair with a TWA Super Constellation over Staten Island and came down here at Sterling Place and Seventh Avenue, striking the Pillar of Fire Church. All 128 people aboard the two airliners and 6 on the ground were killed — 134 in all, then the deadliest aviation disaster in history. An 11-year-old passenger, Stephen Baltz, was thrown clear into a snowbank and survived the impact but died the next day. You can still spot the wound today: look up at 126 Sterling Place and the top courses of brick below the rebuilt roofline are lighter and newer where the DC-8's right wing knifed through, and — unlike its two matching neighbors — its ornamental cornice was never replaced.
properties.photoAlt: Wreckage of the United DC-8 in the street at Seventh Avenue and Sterling Place the day after the December 1960 crash

properties.name: Old Stone House
properties.description: A reconstruction of the 1699 Vechte-Cortelyou House, a Dutch-Colonial fieldstone farmhouse. During the Battle of Brooklyn in August 1776, Maryland soldiers made repeated, doomed charges against British troops holding the house so Washington's army could retreat — the stand later memorialized as 'the Maryland 400.' The original was buried and forgotten, then rebuilt from its excavated stones in 1934. Today it is a small history museum in Washington Park (J.J. Byrne Playground) at 336 Third Street, between Fourth and Fifth Avenues.
properties.photoAlt: The reconstructed Old Stone House (Vechte-Cortelyou House) in Brooklyn, photographed in 1940
properties.photoCredit: Stanley P. Mixon, 1940 · Historic American Buildings Survey, Library of Congress (public domain)
